description: Hello! We are Sirius Team; we develop projects in the fields of artificial intelligence, software development, and autonomous systems. We aim to compete as a team with robust technical infrastructure and rapid prototyping capabilities, enabling you to freely bring your ideas to life.
summary: MARSWEAVE is a safe-walk and route-planning simulator we built for astronauts walking on Mars. We pulled NASA and USGS data into a single map of a 16 × 16 km window of Arcadia Planitia: terrain elevation, a subsurface ice index, surface brightness, dust optical depth and orbiter passes. On top of that map, a decision engine suggests three alternative routes. One is balanced, one detours through a candidate science site, and one is simply the shortest. For every route you can see the distance, time, slope and the hazard zones it crosses, along with a short explanation of why. The walk can be followed in 2D, in 3D, or through the astronaut’s helmet, while oxygen, battery and heart rate update as you go, and a mission report is generated at the end. What makes MARSWEAVE different is that it is honest about its data. Every layer is labelled real, derived, modelled or simulated, and anything we have not loaded is marked “not loaded”. We care about this because the shortest path on Mars is not always the safest one, and a crew needs to see the reasons.
details:
What it does and how it works?

MARSWEAVE helps plan and rehearse a walk on Mars. You pick a goal for the walk (water and ice, geology, terrain survey) and a destination, and the app builds three routes over the same terrain grid. All three use the same A* search and differ only in what they weigh. Alpha balances slope, hazards and radio coverage. Beta detours through the candidate science site that adds the least distance. Gamma looks at distance only. Each route shows its length, time, steepest slope and the hazard zones it crosses, plus a short explanation of how it compares with the others. You can follow the walk in 2D, in 3D, or through the astronaut’s helmet while oxygen, battery and heart rate update live. At the end, an automatic mission report lists the hazard zones crossed, the oxygen and battery result, and the cause if the mission fails. Easy mode keeps things simple; Advanced mode shows every layer and source.

Data

Our study area is a 16 × 16 km window in Arcadia Planitia. We downloaded the real data ourselves from the NASA, USGS and LMD archives using Google Colab, which took a lot of effort because the files are large and come in different formats. We then cut each product down to our window and resampled it to the app’s grid.

Five products are real archive data: elevation (MOLA-HRSC), subsurface ice index (SWIM2), surface brightness (Viking MDIM), dust optical depth (LMD, Mars Year 34) and thermal inertia (THEMIS). THEMIS is used for display only because its mosaic has a seam. Four more items are derived: orbiter passes (NAIF SPICE, MRO) and sun position are computed from ephemeris data, while slope, hazard zones and candidate sites are derived from the elevation model and the other layers. Radiation and weather use published MSL RAD and MEDA values as references. Walking energy, oxygen use and heart rate are modelled (Minetti 2002, NASA PLSS). Relay shadow and storm timing are simulated. CRISM minerals and HiRISE rocks / SHARAD profiles are not loaded.

Benefits and Impact

MARSWEAVE turns data from several missions into something a planner or astronaut can read at a glance, and shows why a route was chosen. We want people to see that the shortest path on Mars is not always the safest, and to make the trade-offs between time, terrain risk and science value clear before a walk begins.

Tools

We built the app with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4 and Three.js, and used Python in Google Colab to fetch and process the data. The app runs in a normal web browser, so no special hardware is needed.

What is creative about it?

First, honesty is a feature. Every layer is labelled real, derived, published, modelled or simulated, and data we have not loaded (CRISM, HiRISE, direct SHARAD) is shown as “not loaded” instead of being faked. Second, route planning follows the purpose of the walk, so the same terrain gives different routes depending on whether the crew is after ice, geology or a terrain survey.

What we considered?

We tried not to claim more than the data supports. The elevation grid is 50 × 50 cells of about 322 m, the ice index is coarse (about 3 km), and the dust data covers a 5° × 6° region, not just our window. Candidate sites come from fixed rules, not detections. Crew and suit mass are assumptions and are labelled as such. We also tested 270 start, target and profile combinations: every route reaches its goal, and Gamma is never longer than the others.
